column7: An Optical Wireless (OW) ISAC scheme [C7: p.1/Intro "optical wireless (OW)-ISAC scheme"] based on Asymmetrically Clipped DC-biased Optical Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (ADO-OFDM) [C7: p.1/Intro "asymmetrically clipped direct-current-biased optical orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (ADO-OFDM)"] using Intensity Modulation and Direct Detection (IM/DD) [C7: p.1/Intro "compatible with the intensity modulation and direct detection (IM/DD) scheme"]. The OW-ISAC transceiver (implemented on a LiDAR) communicates with a separate OWC receiver [C7: p.2/Sec.II "OW-ISAC transceiver is implemented on a LiDAR", "communicating with OWC receiver"]. The transceiver uses one photodetector (PD) for sensing (via reflected signal) and the OWC receiver uses its own PD for communication [C7: p.2/Fig.1 "Photo-detector" for sensing path, "Photo-detector" for OWC receiver].
column8: Previous OW-ISAC schemes are limited in communication rate and flexibility [C8: p.1/Intro "limited in communication rate and inflexible"]. DCO-OFDM wastes power on a DC bias that does not contribute to sensing or communication [C8: p.1/Intro "DC bias neither carries communication data nor contributes to target sensing"]. ACO-OFDM suffers from severe clipping noise, deteriorating spectral efficiency [C8: p.1/Intro "deteriorated spectral efficiency due to the severe clipping noise"]. The joint resource allocation problem is non-convex [C8: p.1/Intro "non-convex joint optimization problem"].
column9: The system performs active sensing (distance estimation) of the OWC receiver [C9: p.2/Sec.II "actively estimates the distance to OWC receiver"] using the reflected signal's Time of Flight (ToF) [C9: p.3/Sec.III.B "estimation of $\tau_0$"]. The Bussgang theorem is used to model and analyze the clipping noise [C9: p.1/Intro "Bussgang theorem is adopted to model the clipped OFDM signal"]. The communication receiver uses Successive Interference Cancellation (SIC) to mitigate clipping noise [C9: p.2/Sec.III.A "successive interference cancellation (SIC) method can be adopted"].
column10: Performance is evaluated by the trade-off between communication spectral efficiency (C, in bps/Hz) [C10: p.3/Eq.11, p.5/Fig.3 "spectral efficiency... C", "Spectral efficiency C (bps/Hz)"] and sensing precision (in cm), which is based on the Cramér-Rao Bound (CRB) and Fisher Information (I) [C10: p.3/Sec.III.B, p.5/Fig.3 "Cramèr-Rao Bound (CRB) is derived as the lower bound for the sensing precision", "Precision (cm)"]. A weighted-sum objective function ($\rho$) balances the two metrics [C10: p.1/Intro, p.3/Eq.20a "objective is in a weighted-sum form", "$\Xi = \frac{\rho C}{C_0} + \frac{(1-\rho)I}{I_0}$"].
column11: Proposes an ADO-OFDM-based OW-ISAC scheme [C11: p.1/Intro "ADO-OFDM-based scheme... for OW-ISAC"]. Formulates adaptive resource allocation as a joint optimization problem [C11: p.1/Intro "adaptive resource allocation... formulated as a joint optimization problem"] and decomposes it into two sub-problems: (1) DCO-ACO power distribution and (2) subcarrier power allocation, which are solved iteratively [C11: p.1/Intro "decomposed into two sub-problems... iteratively solving these sub-problems"].
